Documentary Hypothesis (JEDP)
dok-yoo-MEN-tuh-ree hy-POTH-uh-sis
noun phrase (academic theory)
Standard label for the higher-critical reconstruction of the Pentateuch as a composite of four post-Mosaic sources: the Yahwist (J, from German Jahwist), the Elohist (E), the Deuteronomist (D), and the Priestly source (P). Codified by Julius Wellhausen, Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels (Berlin, 1878).

📖 Biblical Definition

The documentary hypothesis is the central output of 19th-century German higher criticism of the Pentateuch — the theory that Genesis through Deuteronomy is not a unified Mosaic composition but a redaction of four post-Mosaic source-documents (J, E, D, P) compiled over roughly seven centuries (c. 10th to 5th century BC) by successive editors. Julius Wellhausen's 1878 Prolegomena codified the standard form; the theory became the dominant academic position for nearly a century. The Reformed-confessional position holds Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch on the canonical self-witness (Exod 17:14; 24:4; 34:27; Num 33:2; Deut 31:9, 24-26) and on the Lord Jesus's own attribution (Mark 12:26 'in the book of Moses'; John 5:46-47 'Moses... wrote of me'; Luke 24:44 'in the law of Moses'). It rejects JEDP on three grounds: (1) the canonical self-witness is authoritative; (2) the criteria by which JEDP was constructed (different divine names, supposed doublets, supposed contradictions) have been internally criticized within secular academic Old Testament studies since the 1970s, and many specialists now regard the classical hypothesis as collapsed; (3) the late dates Wellhausen assigned to the P source for theological reasons have been refuted by archaeological discoveries (Hittite treaty parallels for Deuteronomy; Late Bronze Age tabernacle materials; etc.) since World War II. The dictionary rejects JEDP on biblical, intra-academic, and archaeological grounds. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this entry rebuts JEDP by name.

Central 19th-century higher-critical theory of the Pentateuch as a composite of four post-Mosaic sources (J, E, D, P); codified by Wellhausen 1878; rebutted by canonical self-witness + Lord Jesus's attribution + intra-academic collapse since the 1970s + archaeological refutation of late dating.

DOCUMENTARY HYPOTHESIS (JEDP), noun phrase. Central output of 19th-century German higher criticism.

Theory: Pentateuch composed of four post-Mosaic source documents — Yahwist (J), Elohist (E), Deuteronomist (D), Priestly (P) — redacted over roughly the 10th to 5th centuries BC.

Codified: Julius Wellhausen, Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels (Berlin, 1878).

Status: Dominant academic position from c. 1880 to c. 1970; internal academic criticism (Whybray, Rendtorff, Van Seters, the 'collapse of the documentary hypothesis') has eroded the classical hypothesis since the 1970s; no replacement consensus has emerged.

Rejected by the dictionary on biblical, intra-academic, and archaeological grounds; Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch is the dictionary's confessional position.

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 17:14 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book."

Deuteronomy 31:24-26 — "And it came to pass, when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished, That Moses commanded the Levites, which bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD, saying, Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee."

John 5:46-47 — "For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me. But if ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words?"

Luke 24:44 — "And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The documentary hypothesis is itself a corruption pattern that the dictionary names and rebuts. The Pentateuch is the work of Moses, attested by the canonical self-witness and by the Lord Jesus's own attribution, against the late-19th-century academic reconstruction.

expand to see more

Canonical self-witness over academic reconstruction. The Pentateuch repeatedly identifies Moses as its author or as the recipient of its commands to write (Exod 17:14; 24:4; 34:27; Num 33:2; Deut 31:9, 24-26). The Lord Jesus repeatedly attributes the Pentateuch to Moses (Mark 12:26; John 5:46-47; Luke 24:44). The apostle Paul does the same (Rom 10:5). The choice between JEDP and Mosaic authorship is not the choice between two scholarly hypotheses; it is the choice between trusting Wellhausen's 1878 reconstruction and trusting the Lord Jesus's stated assumption. The dictionary chooses the Lord Jesus's stated assumption. # voice-lock-ok: histcrit: this paragraph rebuts JEDP on its merits.

Intra-academic collapse since the 1970s. The classical Wellhausen hypothesis has been increasingly criticized within secular academic Old Testament studies for fifty years. R.N. Whybray (The Making of the Pentateuch, 1987) demonstrated that the criteria by which JEDP was constructed (different divine names, supposed doublets, supposed contradictions) do not in fact support the four-source partition. Rolf Rendtorff and John Van Seters proposed major revisions or replacements. The current academic state is one of dispersed micro-hypotheses without consensus; the classical confidence of 1878 to 1970 has eroded. The Reformed-confessional reader notes that this internal academic collapse corroborates from the inside what the apostolic-Lord's-attribution had said all along.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Central 19th-century higher-critical theory of the Pentateuch as composite of J, E, D, P sources; codified by Wellhausen 1878; rebutted by canonical self-witness, Lord Jesus's attribution, intra-academic collapse since 1970s.

expand to see more

Theory: Pentateuch composed of four post-Mosaic sources — Yahwist (J), Elohist (E), Deuteronomist (D), Priestly (P)

Codified: Julius Wellhausen, Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels (Berlin, 1878)

Predecessors: Jean Astruc (1753, observed two divine-name strands in Genesis); de Wette (1805, Deuteronomy as late composition); Hupfeld (1853, four-source theory)

Internal academic criticism: R.N. Whybray (1987); Rolf Rendtorff; John Van Seters; the so-called 'collapse of the documentary hypothesis' literature since the 1970s

Reformed-confessional rebuttals: O.T. Allis (The Five Books of Moses, 1943); R.K. Harrison (Introduction to the Old Testament, 1969); E.J. Young; Duane Garrett (Rethinking Genesis, 1991)

"The documentary hypothesis — the central 19th-century higher-critical theory of the Pentateuch; rebutted by canonical self-witness and intra-academic collapse alike."
